title: Do You Need a VPN in India? What It Does and Doesn't Do
html:
Most people do not need a VPN for everyday browsing. A VPN encrypts the traffic between your phone and the VPN's server, which can help on a public Wi-Fi network, but it does not make you anonymous and it does not stop phishing or malware. It also moves trust: the VPN company can see what your own internet provider would have seen. So the question is not "which free VPN is best" but "do I need one, and do I trust this company".

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. Rules and apps change; the sources are linked.

Sources last checked: 10 Oct 2026.

What a VPN does

Google describes its own VPN as encrypting your device's internet traffic, so that it hides your data and activity from hackers on public Wi-Fi and from unfamiliar internet providers. Other VPNs work on the same idea: your traffic goes through the VPN's server before it reaches the website.

What it does not do

  • It does not stop a website or app you sign in to from knowing who you are. Google makes the same point about its own VPN: it does not change the data other Google products collect from you.
  • It does not protect you from a phishing page you type your password into, or from a harmful app you install. See how to spot phishing.
  • It does not make you immune from the VPN company itself. All your traffic passes through its servers.

VPN by Google is not offered in India

Google's help page says Pixel 7 and later phones have a built-in VPN by Google "in countries where VPN is available". The page lists 32 countries. India is not among them. If you read a guide that tells you to turn it on in India, it is out of date.

What India's CERT-In rules say about VPN providers

On 28 April 2022 CERT-In, India's computer emergency response team, issued directions under section 70B of the IT Act. Two of them matter here:

  • Service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations must keep logs of their ICT systems for a rolling 180 days, within India.
  • Data centres, VPS providers, cloud providers and VPN service providers must register and keep, for 5 years or longer after the service ends: the validated names of the customers, the period of hire, the IP addresses allotted, the email address, IP address and time stamp used when signing up, the purpose of hiring the service, validated address and contact numbers, and ownership details.

The document says the directions take effect 60 days after issue. In plain terms: a VPN company that serves Indian users can be required to know who its customers are. Whether a particular company follows this, or has chosen to stop serving India, is something we cannot confirm. Ask the company, and read its privacy policy for what it logs.

Free VPN apps

An app that routes all of your traffic through its servers has to be trusted more than most apps. A free app still has to pay for its servers, so find out how it earns. Before you install any VPN app, open its Play Store page and read the Data safety section, check what permissions it asks for, and look at who publishes it. Our guide on checking app permissions shows how.

Setting up a VPN on Android

Get the connection details from the VPN provider, then open Settings, then Network and internet, then VPN. Tap Add, enter the details and tap Save. Many VPN apps set this up for you. Two settings are worth knowing: Always-on VPN keeps the VPN running whenever the phone is on, and "Block connections without VPN" stops traffic from leaving the phone if the VPN drops. Both are in Settings, then Network and internet, then VPN, then the settings icon next to your VPN. If the always-on connection stops working you get a notification that stays until you reconnect.

What to do next

  1. Decide why you want a VPN. If it is only to stay safe on public Wi-Fi, use mobile data instead when you can.
  2. If you use one, check who runs it and what it logs before you install it.
  3. Never rely on a VPN to protect an account. Use 2-step verification: see our guide.
